ears_syntax.guidance: Every functional requirement must be written in exactly one of these six patterns. The patterns constrain natural language so requirements are observable and falsifiable.

pattern.name: Ubiquitous
pattern.applies_when: Behavior that is always active under all conditions. No trigger and no state, therefore no keyword.
pattern.example: The mobile phone shall have a mass of less than 150 grams.

pattern.name: State-Driven
pattern.applies_when: Behavior active for as long as a specified state remains true.
pattern.example: While there is no card in the ATM, the ATM shall display "insert card to begin".

pattern.name: Event-Driven
pattern.applies_when: Response required when a specific triggering event occurs.
pattern.example: When "mute" is selected, the laptop shall suppress all audio output.

pattern.name: Optional Feature
pattern.template: Where <feature is included>, the <system name> shall <system response>
pattern.applies_when: Requirements that apply only to product variants containing a specified optional feature.
pattern.example: Where the car has a sunroof, the car shall have a sunroof control panel on the driver door.

pattern.name: Unwanted Behaviour
pattern.template: If <trigger>, then the <system name> shall <system response>
pattern.applies_when: Required response to undesired situations: faults, failures, errors. Mandatory for every error path.
pattern.example: If an invalid credit card number is entered, then the website shall display "please re-enter credit card details".

pattern.name: Complex
pattern.template: While <precondition(s)>, When <trigger>, the <system name> shall <system response>
pattern.applies_when: Richer behavior needing more than one EARS keyword, including complex unwanted behaviors.
pattern.example: While the aircraft is on ground, When reverse thrust is commanded, the engine control system shall enable reverse thrust.

ears_syntax.clause_ordering: The clauses of a requirement written in EARS always appear in the same order: preconditions, then trigger, then system name, then system responses.

requirement_characteristics.note: The corpus mind map counts nine characteristics; the 2018 standard lists ten. All ten are encoded here.
requirement_characteristics.characteristic: Defines an essential capability; removing it leaves a deficiency no other requirement covers.
Level of detail matches the level of the entity it governs.
Needs no further elaboration to be understood and acted on.
States one capability, characteristic, constraint, or quality factor.
Realizable within system constraints at acceptable risk.
Provable by Test, Demonstration, Inspection, or Analysis.
Accurately represents the stakeholder need it derives from.
Follows the approved template and style, here EARS.
Linked upward to its source and downward to design, tasks, and evals.

requirement_identity.rule: IDs are stable across versions. The ID of a deleted requirement is never reused.
Completeness cannot be scored without IDs; an unidentified requirement does not exist for traceability purposes.

traceability.field: Origin of the requirement: a stakeholder, a document, or a standard.
Why the requirement exists and why its priority holds.
P1 to P3. P1 defines the MVP.
One or more observable, falsifiable conditions, linked by requirement ID.
traceability.matrix: Every requirement links forward to design elements in PLAN.md, tasks in TASKS.md, and evals in EVALS.md, and backward to its source. A requirement with no forward links is unimplemented; code with no backward link is unspecified.

formal_methods_vocabulary.guidance: On the Complex route, express critical properties in these constructs alongside their EARS form. They are the bridge to machine checking in the Verification module.
formal_methods_vocabulary.construct: A predicate that must always hold. Example: INVARIANT count : NATURAL & count < Max
Initial values of state variables. Example: INITIALISATION count := 0
State transitions as a precondition plus an atomic action.
Mutable components of the system state.
Predicates constraining constants. Example: PROPERTIES Max = 10
Reusable textual replacement logic grouping sub-predicates.
Encapsulation of the state and operations of a formal model.
What the system must eventually do. Example: whenever a request is received, a response eventually follows.
